messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika grew up in a Pacific Islander family in the United States and spent most of his adult life building himself into someone others trusted: a military aviator when he was young, then later an airline pilot, a husband who was steady, competent, and hard to rattle. The event he returns to in treatment happened during combat decades ago, on an evening mission that had stretched into dusk. The failing light had already made everything uncertain. He was moving with others near a landing zone when helicopter noise pressed low overhead, loud enough to vibrate in his chest and jaw. In the confusion around the aircraft, there was abrupt movement, shouting, bodies dropping and turning, and a tactile detail that fixed itself in him with unusual force: the rough weave of military gear and straps grinding against his hands and forearms as he grabbed, braced, and tried to orient himself. He remembers the hour of it as much as anything—the particular slide from late day into night, when shapes were still visible but safety was gone. When he recalls it now, the same terror comes back with such force that he does not experience it as a story about the past. It is immediate, bodily, and overwhelming.

In the years after leaving combat, Mika did what he had always done with fear and uncertainty: he kept functioning. He transitioned into commercial aviation and built a life with his wife around schedules, flights, and routines that looked successful from the outside. Yet he had begun to notice that certain things could pull him out of the present instantly. The sound of helicopters was the clearest. Even when he knew exactly where he was—driving on a freeway, standing on an airport tarmac, hearing a medical helicopter pass over a hotel on an overnight—his body reacted before he could think. Sometimes the memory arrived whole, without warning, as if his surroundings had opened a trapdoor under him. A rough, scratchy texture could do it too: a certain kind of webbed strap, coarse upholstery, stiff fabric rubbing against his skin. He found himself tugging at collars, avoiding particular jackets, and recoiling from materials he could not easily explain to other people. Dusk was often the worst part of the day. As evening approached, he became more uneasy, as if the hour itself carried danger. At night he felt markedly less safe, even at home with the doors locked.

He has tried to describe to his wife that the memory does not feel like an ordinary memory. It can seem as though it belongs to someone else, to a man he recognizes but cannot fully claim as himself. At other times it breaks over him with total emotional force, and that split leaves him unsettled and ashamed. He has come to believe there is something wrong with him as a person because he cannot file the event away the way he thinks other men did. He says he used to be happy, easier in himself, more open to pleasure. Now he experiences himself as chronically miserable, and he speaks about that change as if it were permanent damage.

The world, in his view, has also revealed itself plainly. He is certain it is dangerous, and he lives accordingly. When he enters a restaurant, briefing room, hotel lobby, or airport terminal, he automatically scans for exits before he takes in anything else. On layovers, he chooses seats with a view of the door and notices who comes in, who stands suddenly, who moves too fast. Sudden movements by other people put him immediately on guard; even a fellow pilot rising quickly from a jump seat or a flight attendant stepping unexpectedly into the galley can make his body tense. These habits have become woven into his working life. In airports full of aircraft noise and constant motion, he remains outwardly composed, but the effort is considerable. At home, his wife has learned that evenings can make him remote and watchful. She has also learned not to reach for him abruptly after dark.

What finally brought him to seek help at 63 was not a single dramatic collapse but the growing sense that his world had narrowed around vigilance, dread, and a private conviction of defectiveness. Recently, after hearing helicopter rotors during an evening hotel stay before a scheduled flight, he was hit so suddenly by the full memory and terror that he spent the night unable to settle, acutely alert to every sound in the corridor, repeatedly checking where the exits were. He completed the next day’s responsibilities, but the strain frightened him. He is coming to treatment because he does not want the rest of his life to be organized around danger and because he misses the man he believes he used to be. What frightens him most is that this is simply who he is now: a man who can never feel safe after dark, never stop bracing for sudden movement, and never get far enough away from that evening to know it is over.
